groups.heading: 1. The idea: buy financial products the way you buy a phone

blocks.html: In 2016 Lalit Keshre was thinking about his second company. He had built an education start-up, Eduflix, that Forbes India says he ran for about two and a half years before folding it in mid-2013 when it did not scale fast enough. Times of India puts his earlier start-up at 2010 and attributes its end to lack of funds. Either way, he knew what a failed company felt like, and he had spent years at Flipkart, where he worked on product. He shortlisted education and finance as the next category, and finance won because, as he told the Times of India, "despite the e-commerce boom, the finance sector was still quite traditional. People only had fixed deposits as options."

The team came together as friends do. Keshre and Harsh Jain had met after graduating from IIT, worked at a start-up, drifted apart and then landed in the same team at Flipkart, per Inc42. They brought in Neeraj Singh, who would become the technology head. Ishan Bansal, who looked at deals for Flipkart's corporate development team, joined after a lunch where he told Keshre he had been thinking about the same problem (Inc42, 2019). Jain put the thesis in a line in 2018: the idea of Groww is "to buy financial products the same way you buy products on Flipkart."

The opening they saw was a gap between money and behaviour. Sequoia India's Ashish Agrawal wrote when leading the Series A that Indians save about 30% of disposable income, much of it in gold, property, fixed deposits or cash, and that fewer than 3% of Indians invested in equities (Forbes India, 2021). The founders did not have a financial-services background. They had a conviction, drawn from e-commerce, that customer experience was missing in the category. They also did not rush. Keshre says it took almost a year to launch because they spent so much time talking to customers on the ground (Inc42, 2019).

The first version of Groww was an advice company. Times of India reports that within six months of setting up, Groww changed from providing a financial coach to providing financial products, after Keshre found there were few takers for coaching. Keshre says users kept asking whether they could buy on the platform. The company dropped coaching and built a catalogue instead.

That catalogue was the bet. In 2017 the usual industry approach was to curate a short list, because too many choices scare a first-time investor. Groww went the other way. Keshre called it "contrarian" to offer 5,000 mutual funds and let customers choose, and the team compensated by giving every fund a page that showed what it held, the expense ratio, who managed it and the manager's record (Inc42, 2021). When the product relaunched in May 2017, Keshre says, it signed up six times the users the team expected in the first month. He calls it the moment they knew it would work.

Being first was never the claim. In 2018 Neeraj Singh answered a question about Paytm and PhonePe entering the category by pointing to Flipkart itself: it was not the first e-commerce company either, and big entrants only validated the idea (YourStory, 2018). Years later at a conference Keshre put it more sharply: "Being first is not important; it's more important to be the last" (YourStory, 2024).

A conflict between two accounts. YourStory reported in February 2018 that Groww earned 1% to 1.5% of assets in commissions from fund houses and that adding direct plans was its next goal. ET's 2025 retrospective says Groww went direct from the start while rivals such as FundsIndia and Scripbox ran regular plans. Both are named sources and they disagree on when the model shifted.

Neeraj Singh described the first build to YourStory in 2020. The team was six: the four founders and two engineers, one of them a former Flipkart colleague and the other a fresher. They needed people who would work for less than the market rate and bring their own laptops. The first version went live with three mutual funds and took two months to build.

For six months the same team ran experiments: customer profiling, a robo-adviser, a risk analysis, and the purchase flow itself. Then they cut. They dropped robo-advice and profiling and expanded from three schemes to every fund from every fund house, again on user feedback. Singh says the team was never satisfied with the product, even though users said they loved the design. The hardest early problem was trust. Nobody had heard of Groww, so the founders answered customer support themselves, talked to users and kept the product stable. People then recommended it to family and friends.

The feedback loop was physical as well as digital. Keshre told TechSparks in 2024 that the team spent hundreds of hours talking to customers, including strangers waiting in cinema queues, and watched facial expressions because polite Indians will not say a product is bad. Groww also ran WhatsApp groups. By early 2018 it had more than 35 of them, and the founders said they expected peer groups to make people comfortable investing (YourStory, 2018). Keshre says 70% to 80% of users came through word of mouth.

A customer in the Forbes India profile shows what they were solving. In 2016 Sonia Chauhan, a young fashion designer in Bengaluru, wanted to invest in mutual funds, but the fast-spoken risk disclaimer at the end of fund advertisements scared her off. The word she remembered was "risk."

Funding followed the traction. The undisclosed seed in January 2018 came from Y Combinator (the US start-up accelerator), Mukesh Bansal, who founded Myntra and Cure.fit, and Ankit Nagori, Cure.fit's co-founder. A pre-Series A of $1.1 million followed in six months. Sequoia India led a $6.2 million Series A in January 2019 and a $21.4 million Series B followed in September 2019 (Forbes India). The September 2020 Series C was $30 million, led by YC Continuity with Sequoia India, Ribbit Capital and Propel Ventures, which took the total raised to $59 million. At that point Groww had more than 8 million registered users for mutual funds and 200,000 stock buyers, and Keshre said more than 60% of users were outside the big cities (TechCrunch).

The unicorn round was $83 million in April 2021, led by Tiger Global (a US investment firm), at a valuation above $1 billion, up from $250 million a few months earlier. Groww had 15 million registered users, two-thirds of them first-time investors (TechCrunch). Six months later ICONIQ Growth led a $251 million round at $3 billion, with Sequoia and Tiger participating (Reuters).

The competition was Zerodha, Paytm Money, Upstox, ET Money and Smallcase, with Zerodha the profitable incumbent that never took venture money (Inc42, 2021). Keshre's answer was a posture, not a tactic. At the unicorn moment he told Inc42 that Groww was "not fighting with" banks and financial institutions but partnering with them to create a market. His stated plan was to deepen the investment products for a year before moving into lending.

Keshre also says Groww made no revenue for its first four years, a strategy he calls delayed monetisation, adding "we're not building this company for today or next year." ET offers a different number: between FY17 and FY20, operating revenue stayed between ₹25 lakh and ₹30 lakh while the active user base grew quickly. Both are named sources, and the gap between zero and a few lakh rupees shows how small the revenue was compared with the user count.

ET reports that Groww secured a stock-broking licence from SEBI (India's securities regulator) in 2019 and launched stock investing in June 2020 (BusinessLine). The timing mattered. As trading opened up during the pandemic years, ET writes, Groww was "at the right place at the right time", and SEBI's move to digital customer onboarding helped. In 2021 Zerodha had around 3.4 million active traders and Groww 0.7 million. In September 2023 Groww passed Zerodha with 6.6 million against 6.4 million.

Two things explain the climb in ET's account. One was brand: Groww used video where Zerodha used text education, and its YouTube channel has 2.4 million subscribers against about 740,000 for Zerodha. Keshre said the company never worked with financial influencers. The other was the word of mouth that had worked for funds: an industry executive told ET that first-time traders heard to "try Groww." Paytm and PhonePe, the two large payments companies, stayed on banking and payments, which left wealth management open to Groww.

Broking brought profits. ET reports that Groww closed FY25 with revenue above ₹4,000 crore and a net profit of ₹1,819 crore. A first-time investor who came for an index fund in 2017 was by 2021 able to trade futures and options on the same screen.

groups.heading: 6. The regulator, the flip and the cost

blocks.html: Two shocks tested the company. The first was structural. Groww had been incorporated in the US, like many Indian start-ups with American investors. In May 2024 it moved its legal home to India in a reverse flip (a move of a company's holding structure back to India) and paid about $159 million in tax. TechCrunch notes that the previous year showed a net loss of about ₹8 billion, mainly from expenses tied to the relocation, while the year to March 2025 showed profit after tax of ₹18.2 billion on total income of ₹40.6 billion, up 45%.

The second was regulatory. After SEBI tightened futures and options F&O (derivatives that are contracts on future prices) rules in November 2024, Inc42 reported that derivatives had fuelled 70% to 90% of the incomes of Zerodha, Angel One and Groww, and that trading volumes fell. Groww's own management said its F&O customer penetration fell from 18% in November 2024 to 10% in the March 2026 quarter, per Medianama's report of the earnings call, with customers instead joining through mutual funds and ETFs.

The company had pushed ahead anyway. In October 2025 it completed the purchase of wealth platform Fisdom (a Bengaluru wealth platform), opening a business for affluent customers under the name W. The DRHP said more than 2.7 lakh active affluent users held portfolios above ₹25 lakh, a segment that had grown nine-fold between FY23 and the June 2025 quarter (BusinessLine, citing the DRHP). ET framed the risk: wealth management is relationship-driven and Groww, a do-it-yourself platform, would have to build offline capacity and compete for relationship managers whose pay had risen 50% to 100%.

Groww filed its draft prospectus in September 2025 with an IPO of fresh shares and an offer for sale. TechCrunch notes that four investors, Peak XV Partners, Y Combinator, Ribbit and Tiger Global, were selling about 394 million shares, roughly 9.4% of the equity, while the four founders were selling about 4 million, 0.7% of the offer. The company listed on 12 November 2025 with a price band of ₹95 to ₹100 and a planned raise of ₹6,600 crore, which at the top of the band valued it at ₹62,332 crore (ET). ET listed the challenges on listing day: reliance on broking, a crowded wealth market and the regulator's focus on speculative trading.

On 14 October 2026 Groww reported results for the quarter to September (the Q2 shareholders' letter and earnings pack are on its investor site, with a Financial Express summary). Revenue from operations was ₹1,501.53 crore, up 47.4%, and profit was ₹724.70 crore, up 53.8% on the year and 1.3% lower than the June quarter. EBITDA margin was 64.5%. Total transacting users reached 2.406 crore, up 26.6%, and customer assets ₹3.89 lakh crore, up 45.7%. Of those users 1.815 crore are active, defined as having transacted in three months or holding assets. Groww says its share of retail stock turnover rose to 15.4% from 12.9%, its mutual fund SIP inflow share to 14.8% from 13.1%, and its margin-lending share to 2.7% from 1.6%.

The notable line is the income mix. Equity derivatives were 56.9% of total income a year ago and 44.8% now. Margin lending (MTF, loans against shares) rose from 4.7% to 10.1%, and commodity derivatives from 0.2% to 6.2%.

blocks.html: The company attributes the derivatives drop to the new closing auction system (CAS), under which SEBI replaced the earlier volume-weighted average price method with a 20-minute auction from 3:15 to 3:35 pm for F&O-eligible shares from 3 August 2026. Equity derivatives revenue fell 14.3% from the June quarter, which Groww says matches the industry. Groww says it expects activity to normalise if SEBI adopts a consultation paper that would separate derivatives settlement from the closing auction price. BusinessLine records that SEBI's advisory panel backed keeping the existing 30-minute VWAP method, leaving the CAS-linked formula on hold. The two positions describe the same open question from different sides.

Growth in the other lines shows where the company is spending effort. Groww AMC, its mutual fund arm, held ₹7,179 crore of assets, up 145.2%, and wealth assets crossed ₹10,000 crore at ₹10,789.66 crore (earnings pack). In September 2026 NSE data showed Groww with 1.34 crore active clients, a 29.16% share of the market, adding 1.01 lakh in the month against Zerodha's 67.92 lakh, which fell by 5,313, and Angel One's 67.56 lakh, which rose by 36,956 (Inc42).

items: Kill the feature your users do not use. The coaching product, the robo-adviser and the customer profiling were all dropped within the first year, and each cut moved the product towards the one thing users asked for: choose and buy.
Treat distribution as the product. Customer support run by founders, WhatsApp groups and word of mouth produced 70% to 80% of users, at a time when the company says it had little revenue.

The unit that carries the margin can also carry the risk. A year ago derivatives were 56.9% of income. When a rule changed the product's economics, the company's answer was mix: margin lending, commodities, an asset manager and a wealth business.

A volume metric needs a quality metric. A platform paid on trading activity earns most from the most active traders. In the multitask framework of Holmström and Milgrom, a reward on the measured task (volume) pulls attention from the unmeasured one (investor outcomes). The F&O share fall from 18% to 10% of customers and the growth of SIPs show a business tilting back towards the second.

For your own work. Insurance aggregators face the same shape. Commission measures the sale and is easy to count; fit, claim support and persistency are hard to count. IRDAI's current paper tries to put measures on the second group.

12.title: Zerodha: built without a rupee of outside money
12.fact: A company story in about 20 minutes. Two brothers, sons of a Canara Bank employee, built India's second-largest broker by active clients with no investors and no advertising. This week it sits 35,830 clients ahead of losing the number two spot it has held since 2023, and a promise it made in 2010 is on the table.

blocks.html: Nithin Kamath was a below-average student who discovered the markets by accident at seventeen. What followed was the standard trader's education: he borrowed money in the early 2000s and blew up his account. To repay the debt he spent four years at a US call centre, selling everything from mobile phones to DVDs on the night shift, trading Indian markets by day. He met his wife Seema on that floor. He left only when the first person asked him to manage a portfolio, and he has said he learnt more about work in those three years than anywhere since: in Zerodha's first two years he was still cold-calling customers himself. "Not everyone can just pick up a phone and make a call," he told YourStory. "I think I've had the most fun in my life during my call centre days."

The detail that matters for everything after: he went bust twice. A founder who has personally blown up a trading account builds a different kind of brokerage, one that warns customers about leverage instead of selling it to them.
Source: YourStory, Matrix Moments interview / CNBC-TV18, Nithin essay

groups.heading: 2. The crash that paid for the licence

blocks.html: By 2005, Nithin was running a franchise of a bigger broking firm, the standard route for a sub-broker in that decade. Then came 2008. The crash that wiped out a generation of traders was, for him, the best market he had ever traded: "In 2008, when there was slowdown and markets fell, he made a little bit of money," YourStory records, "it was just enough to get a licence." The profits from that crash became the deposit for a broking membership. His younger brother Nikhil joined as co-founder; their father was a Canara Bank employee, and neither brother finished college.
Source: YourStory / BusinessLine profile

Operations began on 15 August 2010. The name joined Zero to Rodha, the Sanskrit word for barrier: zero barriers to cost, support and technology, as the company's own about page still puts it. The pricing was the barrier-breaker: a flat ₹20 per executed trade, at a time when established brokers charged a percentage of each trade's value. For an active trader, the saving ran to roughly ninety per cent.

What made a discount broker possible at all was the exchange itself. In an essay published on 11 September 2026, sixteen years in, Nithin spelled out the debt: "Back in 2010, one of the reasons we even considered becoming a brokerage firm was because of NSE NOW. It was a free trading platform provided by the NSE that brokers could offer to their clients." The brothers had no money to build technology. When they went to Chennai to ask about membership, the exchange, on realising how little they had, waived the membership fee of about ₹5 lakh. "In many ways, we are around only because of the NSE," he wrote. "If there is one company I personally feel a sense of obligation towards, it is the NSE."
Source: zerodha.com/about / Nithin Kamath, 11 Sep 2026 / FactorDaily Outliers transcript

For its first four years Zerodha served day traders, and it grew on word of mouth alone. Then the founders ran the arithmetic that changed the company. "India does not have more than 300,000 to 400,000 people who actually speculate," Nithin told YourStory. "We realised that we can't build a business just on this." A flat-fee broker for speculators had a ceiling of a few lakh customers, and every rival was fishing the same pool.

The decision that followed defines the company: stop selling to speculators and start building for investors who had never traded at all. That meant education instead of advertising, and technology built in-house instead of bought from vendors. "Until then, it was all vendor-based products; there was no tech in house, and the only tech I had done was excel sheets," Nithin admitted.
Source: YourStory

Kailash Nadh joined around 2014-15 as chief technology officer and pushed the company to build for the new-age user. The first fruit was Kite, Zerodha's own trading platform, in December 2015: the first product the company had ever built itself. The team behind it stayed famously small; in 2020 Nithin was still marvelling that a thirty-person tech team ran the whole stack, and that barely anyone in the first hundred employees had left. Karthik Rangappa, who took the photograph at the top of this story, joined in 2014 and wrote Varsity, the markets curriculum, single-handedly; it is now among the most-read capital-market education resources in the world. Together, Varsity and the product were the entire marketing budget. "We have achieved this without ever advertising, or raising any external capital or debt," Nithin wrote in 2021.

groups.heading: 6. Coin: giving up the commission on purpose

blocks.html: On 27 March 2017, Zerodha launched Coin, a direct mutual fund platform, made possible by a SEBI decision to let exchange platforms offer direct plans. Direct plans pay the distributor no commission. Every established distributor fought them for years; Zerodha switched its customers to them by default and charged nothing. It was the flat-fee logic applied to funds: give up the spread everyone else lived on, and make it up on volume and trust. The trust compounded. By the company's own current count, over 1.8 crore clients route over 15% of all Indian retail trading volumes through its platforms.
Source: Z-Connect, 27 Mar 2017 / zerodha.com/about

Zerodha's internal operating system is one sentence long, from Nithin's September 2025 post marking fifteen years of Zerodha: "For many years, I have been looking at a 5-year moving average to see if the business is trending up or not." Quarterly and even annual numbers, he argues, push a founder into wrong decisions at every dip. He is explicit about why he can think this way: "This is possible because we don't have external investors." Ten per cent of everything the company earns goes to the Rainmatter Foundation, started in 2020, for climate and social entrepreneurs. No venture fund would have signed either of those terms, which is rather the point.
Source: Z-Connect, "15 years of Zerodha", 30 Sep 2025

Three honest entries. First, reliability: the platform broke during busy trading periods in 2023, and the company says so itself, noting that 2024 and 2025 were much better, with one minor issue, and that it publishes every incident on a disclosures page without any regulation requiring it. It has since built Kite Backup, an emergency trading service that runs on WhatsApp on a completely separate cloud provider.

Second, the revenue engine. The company that swore off building for speculators ended up earning a large share of its brokerage from exactly that pool, weekly options traders. When the regulator finally curbed the trade, brokerage revenue fell about 40% in a single quarter. The founders do not deny the dependence; the September 2025 post is titled "The risk crystallises."

Third, scale itself. Zerodha's active client base has stopped growing: it shrank by 5,313 in September 2026 while Angel One added 36,956. The gap between the number two and number three broker in India is now 35,830 clients, one decent month for the challenger. Zerodha has held that number two rank since October 2023, when Groww passed it.
Source: Z-Connect / ET, Oct 2025 / Inc42 / CNBC-TV18, 8 Oct 2026

The numbers arrived in sequence. Brokerage revenue fell about 40% in the June 2025 quarter after SEBI's F&O curbs (ET). FY25 profit fell 22.9% to ₹4,237 crore from ₹5,496 crore, and revenue fell 11.5% to ₹8,847 crore (Financial Express, from Entrackr's numbers). And in September 2026 the client count ticked down while both rivals either side grew. The chart below is the standings on the NSE last month.

blocks.html: And yet: cash and bank balances more than doubled in the same bad year, to ₹22,679 crore from ₹10,211 crore. Operating margin improved to 63.78% from 55.25%. The exchanges compute Zerodha's net worth at a little over ₹13,000 crore, with zero debt, against client funds that the net worth covers to more than 50% on any given day, a ratio the company calls unprecedented. A broker whose profit falls 23% while its cash doubles is a broker that was never spending the money in the first place.
Source: Financial Express / ET / Z-Connect

Here is where the story stops being history. The regulators are evaluating whether to stop weekly options completely, the trade that built Zerodha's revenue. In September 2025, Nithin wrote the sentence every Zerodha customer should read twice: "If this were to happen, we would be forced to start charging brokerage for equity delivery trades to make the business tenable. Most of our competitors already charge for delivery trades."

Free delivery was the founding promise, the zero in Zerodha's pitch to a generation of first-time investors. The hedge is already built: a margin trading facility launched nine months ago has about 5% of the market and a book of roughly ₹5,000 crore, and client assets on the platform are about 10% of all retail and HNI money in the country. The philosophy says the five-year average is what matters, and on a five-year average the business is fine. But the promise is repriced one regulation away, and the man who must decide spent January 2024 in a hospital. Fourteen months after his stroke, he wrote that his body was almost back to normal and his mind at about 85%. The company he built is the rare one that can survive its worst case. The question for its sixteenth year is what the promise is worth when the worst case is a regulator's pen.
Source: Z-Connect / ET / nithinkamath.me, recovery

13.title: Policybazaar: the comparison shop that became the seller
13.fact: A company story in about 20 minutes. Three IIM graduates founded Policybazaar in 2008 after one founder's father was mis-sold insurance. It survived a regulator that wiped out 90% of its revenue, became India's largest online insurance seller, and now faces the same regulator's biggest rewrite of how insurance may be sold.
13.intro: The story is chronological, so read it straight through. The numbers are boxed at the end, and every source read is listed.

blocks.html: The idea for India's largest insurance marketplace began with two insults, one professional and one personal. The professional one came in 2006. Yashish Dahiya, then a rising executive who had run the travel portal Ebookers across 13 countries, was exploring a job at the British insurer Admiral Plc (the UK motor insurer behind Confused.com) when he saw its sister business, Confused.com: a website where people arrived confused about what to buy and left with a comparison. 'I was pretty impressed with this model and that is what we are replicating in Policybazaar,' he told IIT Delhi years later (IIT Delhi convocation interview, 2020).

The personal insult was worse. Back in India, his father had been sold insurance policies by a broker that served the insurer and the agent, not the customer. 'Most plans pushed by agents are traditional commission-based plans that benefit them. Once sold, such policies have 60 percent chances of lapsing,' Dahiya told YourStory. India in 2008 had no shortage of insurance; it had a shortage of honest comparison. Policies were sold by agents at kitchen tables, and the buyer could not see the menu.

Dahiya was not a natural corporate man. At IIM Ahmedabad in 1996 he had opted out of campus placements to tutor at home, working two hours a day for more than a job would pay, until his mother warned that his sister's marriage prospects needed him employed. He went through Illinois Tool Works, an INSEAD MBA, Bain & Company in London and the managing director's job at Ebookers before the two insults lined up. He teamed up with Alok Bansal (IIM Calcutta MBA; Mahindra, iGate and GE veteran), met through a common friend, and Avaneesh Nirjar. In mid-2008 he carried his laptop to the office of Sanjeev Bikhchandani (founder of Info Edge, which runs Naukri.com) and showed him a comparison of prices at which Bikhchandani could insure his car. Info Edge's founders wrote what Dahiya recalls as 'pretty much the biggest cheque they'd written at the time': ₹20 crore, in September 2008 (Forbes India, 2018; BusinessLine, 2015).

groups.heading: 2. The comparison shop that could not pay its bills

blocks.html: The first Policybazaar was a pure information business. It listed the policies of more than 30 insurers, let visitors compare prices and benefits, and then sent them to the insurer's own site to buy. Insurers paid about ₹100 per enquiry for those referrals. The economics were brutal: in the summer of 2009, at an annual performance review, an employee told Dahiya the year-old company was spending ₹100 to earn ₹10, and then fainted on the spot. Only 1% of visitors bought anything; the company did about 100 transactions a month and booked ₹6 lakh of revenue in September 2008 against continuous spending on technology, people and marketing (BusinessLine, 2015).

The fix was methodical. The team ran thousands of A/B tests on individual buttons to turn browsers into buyers, and marketing shifted from awareness to conversion. Within a couple of years the company was spending ₹100 to earn ₹50, and traffic grew into the millions of visitors a month. By 2015 BusinessLine could describe Policybazaar as accounting for half of all online life insurance sales in the country, with 1.5 million visitors a month.

Then the company's own referee changed the game. In 2011, the Insurance Regulatory and Development Authority's first web-aggregator rules capped advertising revenue at ₹1 lakh per product per year. Policybazaar's revenue at the time was about ₹20 crore; the cap threatened more than 90% of it. The company restructured painfully, moving out its marketing and call-centre operations and turning itself into a sales and back-office operation for insurers (YourStory, 2021).

The survival lesson Dahiya took was that a marketplace with no transaction is at the mercy of whoever owns the rules. Even in 2011, with commissions on digital sales restricted and advertising revenue banned, he was telling anyone who would listen that the customer base had crossed five lakh and was doubling every year. The company that emerged from the wreckage no longer just showed the menu; it sold the meal. In May 2011, Intel Capital and Info Edge put in ₹60 crore in a venture round; a separate $9 million Series A from Intel Capital and Inventus Capital Partners is undated in the sources (Wikipedia). Nirjar, the third founder, left in the early years; two Forbes India profiles disagree on the year, one saying 2011 and another 2013.

What followed was a decade of escalating cheques. A $5 million Series B in April 2013; a $20 million Series C in May 2014 that brought in Tiger Global, the same year Paisabazaar (the group's credit-score and loan comparison platform) launched; a $40 million Series D in April 2015 led by Premji Invest (Wipro chairman Azim Premji's personal investment vehicle) with Steadview Capital and ABG Capital; and a $77 million Series E in 2017 led by Wellington Management and India Value Fund (now True North), with existing investors Temasek and Premji Invest participating (Forbes India, 2017; Wikipedia). By 2017 the site hosted over 60 million visitors a year, closed about 125,000 transactions a month, and accounted for about 20% of India's life cover and over 7% of retail health insurance (Forbes India, 2017).

In June 2018 SoftBank (the Japanese group behind the Vision Fund) led a $238 million round, $150 million of it its own, making Etechaces Marketing and Consulting, the parent, a unicorn. Flush with capital, Dahiya and Bansal tried to move up the chain into healthcare itself with a vertical called DocPrime, reasoning that generating demand for healthcare would generate demand for health insurance (Forbes India, 2018). Tencent bought 10% at a $1.5 billion valuation in November 2019, and SoftBank added $130 million more in July 2020 (Wikipedia).

The deepest pivot came quietly, in two personnel and licensing moves. In December 2019 Sarbvir Singh (former Waterbridge Ventures and Info Edge executive) took over as CEO of Policybazaar while Dahiya became group CEO. Then, in June 2021, the company took out an insurance broking licence from IRDAI, surrendered the web-aggregator licence it had been born under, and announced 100 offline outlets across India (Wikipedia). The comparison shop was formally becoming a seller, with agents and buildings of its own, a dozen years after founding itself against the agent at the kitchen table.

The logic was arithmetic. As a broker it could earn commissions on the policies it sold instead of fees for the enquiries it passed on, and the offline outlets reached customers who would never finish a purchase online. By FY21, 9.6 million unique consumers had bought over 19 million policies through the platform; it claimed a 93.4% share of the online insurance marketplace, and Paisabazaar held 53.7% of digital credit marketplaces (company figures via YourStory). By FY24 it had served 16.6 million unique insurance buyers since inception, and the company said it processed nearly 25% of India's life insurance and over 7% of retail health cover (Wikipedia, citing Frost & Sullivan; company claims).

On 15 November 2021, at the peak of India's pandemic listing boom, PB Fintech (the listed parent of Policybazaar and Paisabazaar, NSE: POLICYBZR) listed after a ₹5,625 crore IPO priced at ₹980 a share, the top of its band. The debut was strong: the stock opened at ₹1,150, up 17%, and closed its first day at ₹1,205, up nearly 23% (PTI via BusinessLine, 15 November 2021). Two days later it touched ₹1,470, its all-time high. Then the market repriced every loss-making 2021 debut: by June 2022 the shares closed at ₹582.90, 60% below the peak and 41% below the issue price, on a day the stock fell 11.5% after Dahiya sold a stake (Economic Times, June 2022; Forbes India, February 2022). The questions were the usual ones and they were fair: when would the marketing spend convert into profit, and was a company that paid for customers worth platform multiples?
Source: PTI via BusinessLine, listing day / Forbes India, Feb 2022

The answer took three more years. FY24 closed with revenue of ₹3,438 crore (company figures via Wikipedia) and the company's first full-year net profit, ₹64 crore, what the Economic Times called a return to the black (ET, May 2024). The September-2025 quarter showed the model at operating speed, and the June 2026 quarter confirmed it: Q1 FY27 net profit rose 92% year on year to ₹162.9 crore on revenue of ₹1,888.3 crore, up 40%, with the profit margin at 9% against 6% a year earlier (results, 5 August 2026; Moneycontrol, Inc42, Mint). Insurance premium through the platform grew 41% to ₹8,372 crore, led by the protection business Dahiya had preached for a decade: new protection premium up 53%, new health insurance premium up 59%. Paisabazaar added ₹127 crore of revenue, up 25%, with core loan disbursals up 33% to ₹2,776 crore and 60.6 million credit-score consumers (Moneycontrol; Mint).

The honest footnote: sequentially, profit fell 38% from the March quarter's ₹261.2 crore and revenue slipped from ₹2,061 crore, so the curve is not a straight line (Inc42). But the structural argument of the business had flipped. The company that once spent ₹100 to earn ₹10 now earns a 9% margin at scale, because renewals from millions of past policies arrive each year without a matching acquisition cost.

Three entries in the ledger. First, the original model: a pure referral business left them hostage to both insurer budgets and the regulator's pen, and it took the 2011 near-death to force them into transactions. Second, the forays: DocPrime's bet that owning healthcare demand would feed health insurance stayed a sideshow rather than becoming the next engine (Forbes India, 2018; no scale-up has been reported since). Third, timing and price: listing into the 2021 bubble at platform multiples meant public investors who bought the IPO spent years underwater while the company grew into its valuation (Forbes India, 2022). The uncomfortable symmetry of the story is that the company founded against commission-driven selling now earns its keep as the country's largest commission-earning seller; the answer it gives is that comparison and documented advice keep the sale honest, which is precisely the claim the regulator's new draft will test.

Which brings the story to this week. IRDAI's October distribution draft proposes the deepest rewrite of insurance selling since the 2011 rules that nearly killed the company: prices and features shown before any personal details are taken, a ban on dark-pattern design, a documented needs assessment for every sale, and ceilings on first-year commissions of 20% for distribution companies and 25% for agents on life policies, with lower caps on health renewals (Consumer Arena's summary of the draft; comments close 25 October). The agents' federation LIAFI has answered with a demand for commissions up to 35%, legislated (Mint, 17 October). Caught between them sits the largest digital distributor in the country, whose 9% margin is built on exactly the commission economics now under review.

The decision in front of Dahiya and Singh is which side of the table to sit on. Policybazaar can fight the caps alongside the agent force it once disrupted, or it can embrace the needs-based, transparent sale as the final vindication of the 2008 idea and compete on cost to serve. The draft's own logic favours the second path: if every seller must show prices openly and justify the recommendation, the comparison engine becomes the regulatory standard rather than the rebel. What would invalidate that reading: caps compressing take rates faster than the company's cost advantage widens, which will show up first in the September-quarter results now due, and in whether the final rules treat brokers and corporate agents differently. The founders who built a company on a mis-sold policy are about to find out whether the regulator now agrees with them.
Source: Consumer Arena on the draft / Mint on the LIAFI letter

14.title: Zoho: the company that said no
14.fact: A company story in about 20 minutes. Sridhar Vembu and his co-founders built a software company from a Chennai suburb and a New Jersey bedroom, refused venture capital at the top of a bubble, survived a crash that killed over 90% of their customers, and crossed ₹12,313 crore of revenue without ever taking outside money. The question now is whether the model survives AI.
14.intro: The story is chronological, so read it straight through. The numbers are boxed at the end, and every source read is listed.

blocks.html: Sridhar Vembu's origin story is often told from the village, so let us do that quickly and correctly. He was born in 1968 in Umayalpuram, a village in Tamil Nadu's Kaveri delta famous for a mridangam maestro who happened to be his mother's cousin. His father worked in the Madras High Court. Vembu topped his class-12 exams, ranked 27th in the IIT Joint Entrance Examination, went to IIT Madras, then to Princeton for a PhD in electrical engineering, and then did something his degree was not for: in April 1996, in Silicon Valley, he tried to build hardware, blew his life savings, and took a contract job fixing obscure bugs in pre-ANSI C code at a company that had been absorbed by Cisco. 'I had already made up my mind I would never ever use my PhD to get a job,' he wrote years later. 'I wanted to work in the trenches of software' (25-years blog, 2021).

The company he would run was already forming without him. In East Tambaram, a Chennai suburb, his brothers Kumar and Sekar had started a contract software outfit with Shailesh Kumar, who still heads Zoho's engineering. In New Jersey, Tony Thomas, three years Vembu's senior at IIT and working at AT&T Bell Labs, had started a bedroom operation in 1995, helped by a personal loan from his elder brother Joy, writing a Java library for the SNMP protocol that telecom equipment makers use to manage networks. A common friend from IIT introduced Vembu to Thomas; Vembu introduced Thomas to his brothers. The two halves began working together in mid-to-late 1996 (25-years blog).

Vembu's entry into the firm is the scene to remember. In early 1997, Thomas came to Silicon Valley to sell his SNMP software and asked Vembu, over lunch, if he knew anyone who could help. He could not pay anything. Vembu offered himself. There was no job to join, so he manufactured one: he printed business cards for $10 at Office Depot reading 'VP of Marketing and Business Development, Advent Network Management', and staffed the 10x10 booth Thomas had rented at Networld+Interop in Las Vegas. 'To my own surprise and Tony's surprise, I made some sales at that event,' he wrote. 'I was not a good salesman... but then Tony was even worse than me, so by the law of comparative advantage I became the salesman.' Sales in 1997 came to $350,000. Every dollar went back into R&D for the next product, Web NMS. In 1998, sales crossed $1 million and the founders began paying themselves modest salaries; Vembu declared the company 'a real business' only then, because it could put food on the table (25-years blog).

By 1999-2000, AdventNet was selling network-management software into the biggest bubble most of its customers would ever see. The telecom equipment boom was, in Vembu's accounting, bigger than the dotcom bubble the media watched: over a trillion dollars eventually written off between carrier debt and venture capital into equipment startups. He had an unusual vantage point: 'I personally must have visited 80% of those equipment companies, as a software supplier.' He had also read his history, the Japanese bubble of the late 1980s, and he could hear the same pitch repeated by dozens of companies that did not know the others existed (surviving-the-crisis blog, 2008).

In 2000, a venture capitalist offered AdventNet $10 million for a 5% stake, a $200 million valuation for a company heading towards $10 million in sales. The partners turned it down. 'We felt the industry was going to shrink, not grow, and we didn't want to commit to a growth projection when our instinct told us to get ready for contraction,' Vembu wrote. 'One of my friends in venture capital did tell me I was a fool - but that folly saved us.' They did something else that mattered just as much: they did not let headcount chase revenue. 'We simply banked the cash - which came in really handy in the subsequent nuclear winter.' (2008 blog.)

The winter was worse than he imagined. Vembu thought perhaps 20% of the startups would survive; in the event, he reckons three out of more than 200 did. By 2003, over 90% of the companies AdventNet had supplied in 1999-2000 were gone. What saved the company was the boring sequence: no outside money to answer to, cash in the bank, young engineers on payroll. The reinvention came in two steps: ManageEngine, IT-management software for companies rather than equipment makers, born in 2002-03, and Zoho.com, rented business software delivered over the internet, in 2005. 'Indeed, it was that cash that enabled us to diversify in 2004, and that was ultimately what led to Zoho' (2008 blog; 25-years blog).

There is a second, quieter refusal in the record. Some fifteen years before his Forbes India interview in 2016, the one time Vembu entertained a VC term sheet, he read the clause requiring a guaranteed exit or liquidity within seven or eight years. 'There was no way I could guarantee that,' he said. His summary of the whole philosophy: 'Why sacrifice freedom? That is the primary reason. We operate on our own clock' (Forbes India, 2016).

In 2005, the company began an experiment that looks, in hindsight, like its most consequential product. It started hiring teenagers straight out of class 12 from low-income households and training them in-house to build software. The programme became Zoho University, now Zoho Schools. Paramasivam Saran Babu, one of six recruits in the first batch, was trying to finish school at a government 'corporation school' in Chennai while his diabetic father ran a printing press. 'I hardly spoke any English at the time, but I was really good at math... maybe that's why they hired me,' he told Forbes India. Eleven years later he was the product manager for Zoho Creator, a low-code product used from the SRM University next door to the Napa Valley Film Festival, with a team of 30 under him and 60 collaborators (Forbes India, 2016).

The idea was never charity; it was a hiring thesis. 'Formal education only takes you so far, but most of the contextual knowledge comes from actually doing something,' Vembu said. About 15% of the company's employees now come through Zoho Schools, and the company says it is expanding the model to more students, new disciplines and international branches (Forbes India, 2016; Zoho's Our Story page). The same instinct, value in the overlooked, explains the geography. From 2019 the company began breaking its big-campus model into small 'spoke' offices in towns and villages, and in 2021 it said it would hire up to 2,000 people for rural offices (Mint, 2021). Vembu himself moved to Tenkasi, a town in Tamil Nadu's far south, and runs much of his work from there.

groups.heading: 4. No VC, no IPO, no ads

blocks.html: Zoho's operating doctrine reads like a list of things the technology industry considers impossible. It has never raised external capital. It says it will not go public and will not be acquired. It runs its own data centres rather than renting the public cloud. It claims to spend twice as much on R&D as on sales and marketing. It has never sold customer data or shown a third-party ad inside its products, and it removed third-party trackers from its own websites. 'When you think of an operating system, you think of something that runs your device. Zoho has software that runs your business,' Vembu told reporters in 2016 (Our Story; Forbes India, 2016).

The doctrine has a balance sheet attached to it. Revenue went from about $200 million in 2012 (a Bloomberg interview cited by Forbes India) to ₹6,711 crore in FY22 and ₹12,313 crore in FY25, roughly a doubling in three years, with profits every year. The FY25 split: the Zoho business-applications suite contributed 57% of revenue at ₹7,051 crore, ManageEngine 39% at ₹4,863 crore, and services the remaining ₹399 crore. North America is still the biggest market at 41% of revenue (₹5,028 crore), followed by Asia at 30% and Europe at 23%. The company passed 100 million users across more than 55 applications in September 2023 (entrackr; moneycontrol; Business Standard, 2023).

The family around the company matters to how it runs. Brother Kumar, who came back to India in 1997 as president and COO for six years, later founded retail-software maker GoFrugal. Brother Sekar runs Vembu Technologies. Sister Radha runs Zoho Mail; the youngest sibling, Manikandan, is chief operating officer. Tony Thomas, the first CEO, moved out in 2004 but retains his stake. 'He was the superstar in our family,' Radha Vembu says of Sridhar (Forbes India, 2016).

The strongest evidence that Zoho's training culture works is the list of people who left. Girish Mathrubootham joined as a pre-sales engineer in 2001, rose to vice president of product management running ManageEngine, and quit in 2010 to found Freshdesk, the helpdesk startup that became Freshworks and eventually listed on Nasdaq, laying off 11% of its staff in May 2026 as it restructured for AI, a fate Zoho has so far avoided. Other alumni: the founders of Zarget (website testing, backed by Accel and Matrix), of Voonik (fashion e-commerce), and a cluster of Chennai SaaS founders who call themselves, only half-joking, the Zoho mafia. 'The answer is very, very clear in my mind - it was the operational freedom,' Mathrubootham said of what Zoho gave him. Matrix Partners' Tarun Davda backed Zarget largely on that pedigree: 'Zoho is a great training ground' (Forbes India, 2016; Mint, 2026).

The comparison the alumni story invites is instructive. Freshworks raised venture money, went public, and answers to a stock price; Zoho stayed private, and answers to its own clock. In the AI squeeze of 2026, the two Chennai schools are running the same experiment with different constraints: Freshworks cut jobs to protect a margin the market watches, while Zoho froze pay and marketing to protect a workforce nobody can force it to cut (Mint, 14 October 2026).

Every crisis in this story has arrived from the same direction: a technology shift that changed what customers would pay for. Telecom in 2001. Cloud in 2005. Now AI. Zoho saw this one early enough to build: in July 2025 it launched its own foundational model stack, Zia LLM, alongside prebuilt agents, a custom agent builder and speech-recognition models, all run on its own data centres, extending a privacy argument (your data, our metal) into the AI era (Indian Express, July 2025). The consumer bet followed: Arattai ('chit-chat' in Tamil), a homegrown messaging app, went viral last year and hit the number one spot on Indian app stores; on 2 October 2026, a day after Meta started charging businesses for certain WhatsApp service messages, Zoho launched Arattai for business, free for government and public services like the Railways, with a million free messages a month for healthcare and educational institutions (India Today, 2 October 2026).

And yet the same fortnight brought the most telling moment in the company's recent history. On 13 October 2026, Vembu posted on X: 'We have cut down on our marketing budget. We have also told our employees that we cannot have our usual pay increase this year. I have apologized for not being able to avoid this. We will work hard to avoid mass layoffs but the outlook for software jobs in general is grim. We have not been growing our employee count for 18 months now.' He cited a four-fold increase in server prices for AI data centres and a difficult geopolitical backdrop (Mint, 14 October 2026).

The financials show the squeeze arriving in two waves. In FY23, the year generative AI went mainstream, profit rose 3% but employee costs jumped 49%. In FY25, employee costs rose another 29% to ₹4,347 crore, advertising spend rose 31.3% to ₹2,230 crore, depreciation nearly half-again to ₹741 crore as data-centre investment bit, and net profit slipped 3% to ₹3,191 crore on revenue up 17.8% to ₹12,313 crore. The company still spends only ₹0.75 to earn each rupee of revenue, holds ₹1,880 crore of cash, and runs a 31.27% EBITDA margin. This is not distress. It is a margin decision being made early, by choice, which is the whole point of being Zoho (moneycontrol; entrackr; Mint).

What did the company get wrong? Two things are defensible criticisms, not hindsight. First, it hired ahead of the shift: a 49% jump in employee costs in FY23 was a bet that the SaaS expansion would continue, and the 18-month headcount freeze is the admission that it did not. Second, its moat is also its exposure. Zoho's low-price suite sells to small businesses, and consultants note that small clients with little custom data are exactly the customers who can migrate fastest when AI makes cheap internal automation possible. 'Many of its clients are small clients, who aren't too reliant on custom data - and may thus migrate rapidly to cost-effective solutions due to AI,' says YCP India's Abhisek Mukherjee. The counter is 29 years of reinvention: the company that sells the 'operating system for business' is betting it can also be the company that supplies the agents (Mint, 14 October 2026).

The decision scene belongs to Shailesh Kumar Davey, the engineer from the East Tambaram room who became group CEO in January 2025. His inheritance is precise: keep the ₹3,191 crore profit engine funding the AI build-out, hold the 30,000-strong workforce together without the layoffs peers have chosen, and prove that a bootstrapped Indian company can own its models, its data centres and its pricing power at once. Vembu, now chief scientist, has moved himself to the R&D problem that decides it. The company that refused the cheque in 2000 is placing the same bet again: that it is better to be early, own the downside, and answer to no one.

The product he founded was thrown away within 30 days, the company that replaced it became India's 26th unicorn of its year, then hit a wall of its own making, and now faces its public-market verdict on Friday. This is that story, told with the numbers attached.

groups.heading: Part 1: the son of a pivot

blocks.html: There is something about pivoting and the Acharyas. In his early forties, Arabinda Acharya left his insurance job in Bhubaneswar to chase a doctorate mid-career; years later his wife started a non-profit at 58. Their son Amrit grew up watching both bets work. Amrit's own path looked safer from the outside: IIT Madras, then four years at ITC, where his first task was helping build a new factory and where he ended up managing hundreds of suppliers on Google Sheets for close to ₹500 crore of procurement. In 2014 he left for an MBA at UC Berkeley, and in September 2016 he joined McKinsey in San Francisco.

By the end of 2017, one question kept him up: is the unknown a risk or an opportunity? The job was not the problem. "McKinsey was great," he later recalled. But at Berkeley almost nobody had talked about taking a job; everyone talked about building. "The bug bit me and I quit McKinsey. I called up Srinath and started discussing the possibility of building a startup." In January 2018 he came home, part of what the Indian press would later call the Ghar Wapsi wave of founders returning from the Valley. He and Srinath Ramakkrushnan rented a one-bedroom apartment in HSR Layout, Bengaluru, and started.
Source: Moneycontrol, germ of an idea (2023) / Forbes India, the unicorn piece (2021) / YourStory, the turning point (2021)

groups.heading: Part 2: the product they threw away

blocks.html: Zetwerk, founded in May 2018 by Acharya, Ramakkrushnan, Vishal Chaudhary (IIT Kharagpur) and Rahul Sharma, was not a manufacturing company. It was a SaaS tool: software for project managers to manage their existing supply chains better, born directly from Acharya's ITC spreadsheets. The team raised capital for that product, a $1.5 million seed round from Kae Capital and Sequoia. Then they sat with customers. The customers did not want to manage their current suppliers better; they asked whether the software could help them discover new ones. "That was our eureka moment," Acharya has said.

What happened next is the part most founders get wrong. Within months of founding, having raised money for one business, the team went back to its investors and said the business was wrong. "We had raised capital for SaaS, but we went back to investors telling them that we'll start a software business differently. We felt that this marketplace model had a higher probability of success, and the investors supported us." The new Zetwerk would be a marketplace: it would own no factories, employ no machinists, and instead route manufacturing orders, fabricated parts, precision components, later entire projects, to a network of small factories that had spare capacity and no sales force. The factory that owns no factories. In December 2018, Accel and Sequoia led a $9 million Series A into the pivoted company.
Source: YourStory (2021) / Moneycontrol (2023)

groups.heading: Part 3: the fastest three years in Indian manufacturing

blocks.html: The numbers of the early years still read like a misprint. Operating revenue was ₹16 crore in FY19, ₹321.93 crore in FY20, ₹835.5 crore in FY21, and then, pole-vaulting on two global tailwinds, the China-plus-one sourcing shift and an infrastructure push at home, ₹4,961 crore in FY22. That year Zetwerk posted its first operational profit, making it that rare thing, a profitable unicorn. International revenue went from 5% of the total in FY21 to 16% in FY22, with 70% of international orders coming from the US. The funding kept pace: a $32 million Series B from Lightspeed and Greenoaks in November 2019, and in August 2021 a $150 million Series E led by D1 Capital Partners at a $1.33 billion valuation. Three years from a one-bedroom apartment to India's 26th unicorn of 2021.

Acharya's reaction to the milestone tells you something about what came next. Asked about celebrating, he admitted to a long-standing complaint from his teammates: he does not pause. After every milestone, he talks about the next one. The father who left insurance for a doctorate in his forties still did not fully understand what his son did for a living; the son kept his fingers crossed that the unicorn tag would explain it.
Source: Forbes India, the six-fold leap (2022) / Forbes India (2021) / Moneycontrol (2023)

groups.heading: Part 4: what the company got wrong

blocks.html: Every honest company story has a section like this, and Zetwerk's is civil infrastructure. As the company grew, it moved from manufacturing components into large civil construction projects, and the segment became big enough that its unwinding moved the whole company's numbers. In FY25, gross revenue fell 11% to ₹12,798 crore from ₹14,443 crore in FY24, the first decline in the company's history. The loss for the year narrowed 60% to ₹371 crore, helped by a sharp drop in exceptional items, and the company posted a positive EBITDA of ₹145 crore, but the top line had gone backwards. The updated DRHP, filed in August 2026, says plainly what happened: Zetwerk is exiting the civil infrastructure business.

The exit was expensive. In FY26, discontinued operations, the civil business being wound down, contributed a ₹641.8 crore loss on top of a ₹964.4 crore loss from continuing operations, the latter inflated by an ₹835.8 crore exceptional item. Total reported loss for FY26: ₹1,606 crore, the worst headline number the company has ever printed, arriving in the same document that asks the public to buy its shares. And there is one more disclosure a careful reader should not miss: 4.80% of shares held by certain promoter-group members and Creovate Innovation are pledged to Catalyst Trusteeship under non-disposal undertakings. The company itself warns that if lenders exercise those pledges, promoter shareholding could be diluted and the share price affected. Credit to the DRHP for putting all of it on the table; it is also on the reader to actually read it.
Source: Moneycontrol on the UDRHP (Aug 2026) / Entrackr on FY25 (Jan 2026)

Strip out the business being wound down and the remaining company had its best year. Revenue from continuing operations rose 40.43% in FY26 to ₹15,913.3 crore from ₹11,331.9 crore. Adjusted profit before tax turned positive at ₹45.7 crore. Manufacturing Business EBITDA reached ₹565.1 crore, a 6.03% segment margin; company-wide adjusted EBITDA was ₹421.3 crore, a 2.65% margin. The order book, the pipeline of contracted future work, stood at ₹12,370 crore at the end of FY26, up 43% from ₹8,629 crore a year earlier. Cash and bank balances, ₹1,908 crore at the end of FY25, had risen sharply from ₹1,150 crore the year before. The most recent quarter's net loss narrowed 46.4% to ₹733 crore as the civil exit worked through the books. The pattern is the same one from 2018, run in reverse: find the part of the business that does not compound, cut it, and let the part that does compound show through.

On Monday evening, the ₹5,012.3 crore IPO closed: 3.06 times subscribed, with bids for 56.62 crore shares against 18.50 crore on offer. The split inside that number is the whole story of how the market currently reads Zetwerk. Institutions, who read DRHPs for a living, subscribed 4.73 times their quota, including the ₹2,251 crore anchor book that took in Capital Group, BlackRock, Goldman Sachs, Nomura, Société Générale, Manulife and Prashant Jain's 3P India Equity Fund. Non-institutional investors subscribed 1.40 times. Retail investors filled only 73% of their reserved portion, bidding for 2.50 crore shares. The grey market premium on closing day: ₹5 over the ₹151 cap, implying a listing 3.3% above the issue price.

So picture Friday morning. Amrit Acharya, the man colleagues say never celebrates a milestone, will stand at the listing ceremony while the opening print decides what the story of Zetwerk is called. If the stock holds above ₹151, the story is the FY26 fix: 40% growth, positive adjusted profit, a ₹12,370 crore order book, and a manufacturing network for a country that wants to make more things. If it dips below, the story is the FY26 headline: a ₹1,606 crore reported loss, pledged promoter shares, and a retail book that never filled. Both stories are true. That is what the eight years since the one-bedroom apartment in HSR Layout have built: a company big enough that its truth no longer fits in a headline. The son of two people who bet their careers on pivots has made his own biggest bet, that public investors will read the whole document, not just the first number in it. Friday will grade the bet.

16.title: The bond that refused to die
16.fact: Long read, Wednesday 21 October 2026. On 15 October the Supreme Court ordered Yes Bank to honour ₹8,415 crore of AT1 bonds it wrote down to zero in March 2020. This is the story of how a rescue, a legal technicality and six years of litigation collided.
16.intro: In one sentence: India wrote off a failed bank's riskiest bonds to save its depositors, bondholders fought the write-off for six years, and last week the Supreme Court ruled in their favour - leaving a repaired bank with a ₹8,415 crore bill and every AT1 bond in India repriced.

blocks.html: On Thursday 15 October 2026, a two-judge bench of the Supreme Court - Justices Dipankar Datta and Augustine George Masih - dismissed four appeals at once: by Yes Bank, by the administrator who ran it in March 2020, by the Reserve Bank of India, and by the Union of India. With that, the Bombay High Court's January 2023 decision stood: the write-down of ₹8,415 crore of Additional Tier 1 bonds was illegal. The bank must honour the bonds at their original coupons of 9% and 9.5%, plus interest.

The court's reasoning was not that AT1 bonds cannot be written down - they can, that is what they are for. It was narrower and, for the RBI, more uncomfortable. The administrator appointed under the Banking Regulation Act "has to act squarely within the four corners of the powers conferred upon him," the bench held; once the final reconstruction scheme was gazetted on 13 March 2020, he had no power left to write the bonds down. And the court put the supervision failure on record: "The RBI was a mere bystander, allowing the CET1 ratio of YES BANK to drop to an astonishing low of 0.6% while the business of YES BANK was being carried out in a clandestine manner... to have the investors at the receiving end of the administrative lapses would be highly unfair."

The market's verdict was instant: Yes Bank shares fell nearly 20% at the intraday low of ₹16.96 before recovering to close 14.5% lower at ₹18.12. The bondholders' lawyer, Srijan Sinha of Edictum Law & Co., called it what it was - the write-off held "illegal and arbitrary... against the Final Reconstruction Scheme gazetted by the Union of India." Grant Thornton's Vivek Ramji Iyer noted the decision turned "on a technicality rather than the underlying terms of the product" - which is exactly why it matters to every bank in India.
Source: moneycontrol, 15 Oct 2026 / LiveLaw, 15 Oct 2026 / Mint, 15 Oct 2026

Yes Bank was, by early 2020, a study in how fast a growth story can invert. Founded in 2004 by Rana Kapoor and Ashok Kapur, it had become one of India's largest private lenders on aggressive corporate lending. By 2019 the loan book was rotting and depositors were leaving; the RBI had forced founder Rana Kapoor out of the CEO's office the year before. On 5 March 2020 the central government, on the RBI's recommendation, placed the bank under a moratorium - depositors could withdraw no more than ₹50,000 - and superseded its board. The RBI's draft reconstruction scheme, published the next day, said why: "the rapidly deteriorating financial position... relating to liquidity, capital and other critical parameters, and the absence of any credible plan for infusion of capital."

The rescue came together in a week. On 13 March the Union Cabinet approved the scheme; the State Bank of India led a consortium putting in ₹10,350 crore, with SBI alone committing ₹7,250 crore for up to 49%, and ICICI Bank (₹1,000 crore), HDFC Bank (₹1,000 crore), Axis Bank (₹600 crore) and Kotak Mahindra Bank (₹500 crore) alongside. The moratorium lifted within days. Depositors were saved whole. Equity holders kept their shares - 75% of them locked in for three years.

One class of investors got something very different. Late on 14 March, Yes Bank informed the exchanges that its two Basel III Additional Tier 1 bond issues - ₹3,000 crore sold on 23 December 2016 and ₹5,415 crore on 18 October 2017 - "have been fully written down and stand extinguished with immediate effect." The bank cited the RBI's Basel III Master Circular: once Section 45 of the Banking Regulation Act is invoked, the bank is deemed non-viable, and AT1 triggers fire. ₹8,415 crore, gone to zero overnight. AT1 bonds are designed for exactly this - they are the highest-yielding, first-to-die layer of a bank's capital. What the bondholders disputed was not the instrument but the execution.
Source: RBI press release, 6 Mar 2020 (primary) / Indian Express, 13 Mar 2020 / CNBC-TV18, 15 Mar 2020

The holders of those bonds - institutions like 63 Moons, and thousands of individual investors, some of them retirees who said the bonds were mis-sold to them as fixed-deposit-like products - organised under their trustee, Axis Trustee. Before the scheme was finalised they had proposed converting part of the bonds into equity to recover roughly 20% of their money; the RBI turned it down. So they sued.

Their legal argument was surgical. Yes, the draft scheme contemplated a write-down. But the final gazetted scheme of 13 March 2020 did not contain it - and the write-down letter came on 14 March, after the scheme was in force, signed by an administrator whose powers, by then, were only those the statute gave him. On 20 January 2023, the Bombay High Court agreed. It quashed the write-off without ruling on the merits of AT1 instruments: the decision "was not a part of the final restructuring scheme and the administrator did not have the authority to make the decision." Yes Bank, the administrator, the RBI and the government all appealed to the Supreme Court. The appeals sat for nearly three years.
Source: Reuters, 20 Jan 2023 / CNBC-TV18, 15 Mar 2020

While the appeals waited, Yes Bank rebuilt. Under CEO Prashant Kumar, the SBI-installed administrator-turned-chief executive, the bank cleaned its book, raised capital, and returned to steady profitability. By 2025 it was attractive enough to draw India's largest cross-border banking deal: Japan's Sumitomo Mitsui Banking Corporation agreed in May 2025 to buy 20% for roughly ₹13,500 crore, and in August the RBI cleared SMBC to go up to 24.99%. Vinay Tonse, a career SBI banker, took over as MD & CEO. For the September 2026 quarter the bank reported a standalone net profit of ₹1,080 crore, up 65% on the year.

The question nobody could answer until last week: did SMBC's ₹13,500 crore price tag assume the AT1 bonds stayed dead? The Supreme Court has now said they do not. The bank's pro forma CET1 - 13.7% reported at the end of September - drops to about 11.4% once the ₹8,415 crore principal is reinstated, a 240-basis-point hit including profits, per management's own analyst call on Monday. The bank's disclosures go further: recognised as of 30 September, the judgment turns that quarter's ₹1,080 crore profit into a ₹5,217 crore pro forma loss - a figure the bank stresses is not recognised in the reported results and is subject to revision as the legal and accounting treatment is settled.

groups.heading: 5. The decision now on Vinay Tonse's desk

blocks.html: What the court ordered is not a fine but a resurrection: the bonds live again, with their 9% and 9.5% coupons and six years of unpaid interest. On Monday's post-earnings call, CFO Niranjan Banodkar laid out the bank's position with unusual precision. A CET1 of 11-11.5% is "not ideal... we would want more comfortable capital levels irrespective of what the regulator says." But the bank has levers: deferred tax assets, a security-receipts portfolio with a face value of about ₹1,500 crore and an estimated NAV of ₹2,000 crore carried on the books at zero, the ability to grow about 11% without consuming capital, and two rating agencies - one international, one domestic - that have called the verdict credit-neutral. CEO Tonse's summary: there is "no gun to our head" to raise capital; whether to raise now or later is "a commercial evaluation."

That is the decision scene this saga ends on - for now. A management that says it does not need capital, sitting on a bond liability that pays 9-9.5% plus back interest, in a rate cycle where the RBI is hiking. The bondholders, after six years, get their bonds back. The bank gets a recurring coupon bill and a thinner capital cushion. And every other Indian bank's AT1 investors got something quietly valuable: a Supreme Court confirmation that a write-down must be executed with procedural perfection, or it does not happen at all.
Source: Business Standard, 20 Oct 2026 / moneycontrol, 19 Oct 2026

Three failures made this saga. The original sin was underwriting: the lending binge of the 2010s that left CET1 at 0.6% by early 2020 - with the supervisor, in the Supreme Court's words, "a mere bystander." The second was distribution: high-yield perpetual bonds sold to retail investors who say they were told these were safe, deposit-like products, a mis-selling scandal that ran parallel to the legal one. The third was procedural: the 14 March 2020 write-down letter, signed one day too late by an administrator whose powers had already lapsed into the final scheme. A ₹10,350 crore rescue survived every challenge. The piece that failed was one sentence of legal process - and it cost ₹8,415 crore.
